query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Friction‐induced oxide film spallation, dominated by the cyclic formation and brittle breakage of Fe3O4/Cr2O3-rich scales, exposes microgalvanic interfaces that accelerate the coupled wear–corrosion degradation in multiphase eutectic HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: A laser‐fabricated multiphase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with heterogeneous lamellar microstructure (FCC + BCC/B2 phases) and an initially oxide‐free surface.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to high-temperature reciprocating sliding wear (e.g., 850 °C) in ambient air without any pre-treatment to form a stable oxide film.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (850 °C), cyclic sliding contact with controlled load and frequency, ambient atmospheric conditions with controlled humidity, and a test duration long enough to allow oxide film formation/spallation cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: A friction-induced oxide layer that forms predominantly as Fe3O4 and Cr2O3, which initially reduces friction but, under cyclic shear, accumulates stress and spalls off at phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating rapidly oxidizes exposed surfaces producing a transient Fe3O4/Cr2O3 film; however, the cyclic shear and thermal fluctuations exceed the film’s adhesion limits, causing spallation. The consequent exposure of distinct phases creates active microgalvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion. This degradation feedback loop couples mechanical wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a pre-oxidized baseline with a stabilized oxide layer, the untreated sample will exhibit a 30–50% increase in total degradation, evidenced by a higher wear depth and increased density of corrosion pits, particularly localized at phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: A matched eutectic HEA sample pre-treated by controlled pre-oxidation at moderate temperatures to form a continuous and adherent oxide film.
generation.boundary: Applicable under thermo-mechanical loading at 850 °C in ambient air; not expected in environments with aggressive molten salts or significantly lower temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: Exact kinetics of oxidation and spallation, including the detailed adhesive strength of the Fe3O4/Cr2O3 film, may vary with slight changes in alloy composition and processing; however, the overall mechanism remains valid.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set receives a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form a stable protective oxide film; the other is left untreated. Subject both to identical reciprocating wear tests at 850 °C. Use in situ high-temperature optical microscopy and post-test SEM/XRD analysis to monitor oxide film integrity, spallation events, and corrosion pit distribution.
measurements: Corrosion pit density and spatial distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the untreated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (>20%) increase in wear and corrosion degradation compared to the pre-oxidized baseline, or if the oxide film does not show cyclic spallation leading to preferential phase boundary exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 13b presents a schematic diagram of the CoCrFeNiMo coating’s wear mechanism. During the sliding wear process, the high-speed friction between the Si3N4 ceramic ball and the HEA coating generated substantial frictional heating, gradually elevating the contact temperature. This thermal activation promoted the reaction between atmospheric oxygen and the elements in the HEA coating, resulting in the formation of a protective oxide layer. Wang et al. [], through Raman spectroscopy, found that the oxides were mainly composed of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, with the presence of MoO3, NiO, Cr2O3, and Co3O4 as well. Among these, Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 played a positive role in the tribological properties of the HEA coating by reducing the coefficient of friction and enhancing frictional stability. However, prolonged testing induced progressive stress accumulation within the oxide layer, triggering adhesive wear at the tribo-interface. As the experiment advanced, cyclic shear stresses fragmented the oxide film into abrasive debris. Deprived of oxide protection, the hard σ-phase particles underwent brittle spallation during subsequent sliding, generating micron-scale pits that accelerated material loss.

For the investigation of the phase constitution within the wear tracks, additional XRD measurements were conducted. The resulting diffractograms are shown in Figure 6. In comparison to the unaffected state (Figure 3), additional diffraction peaks can only be observed for the two highest test temperatures. This behaviour confirms an increased oxide-layer thickness, which is in accordance with the results of the wear tests. The additional maxima can be assigned to a spinel (structure type MgAl2O4). The intensity of the diffraction peaks increases for the sample tested at a maximum temperature of 900 °C. Furthermore, an additional intensity maximum occurs at 59.9°, which could not be assigned. No diffraction peaks of other oxides were detected. The results of the phase analyses differ in comparison to previous investigations on the oxidation behaviour of the alloy system AlCoCrFeNiTi. Wang et al. revealed the formation of mainly TiO2 and (Al0.9Cr0.1)2O3 at an oxidation temperature of 900 °C. papers.title: Influence of Laser Power on CoCrFeNiMo High-Entropy Alloy Coating Microstructure and Properties.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy coating fabricated by laser cladding
papers.approach: Examined the effect of varying laser power (2000–2500 W) on phase evolution and microstructure; coupled wear tests with microstructural characterization.
papers.findings: Under sliding wear, frictional heating promoted rapid oxidation, forming a protective oxide film (containing Fe3O4 and Fe2O3, along with other oxides) which initially lowered friction but later accumulated stress and fractured, leading to adhesive wear and brittle spallation of hard σ-phase particles.
papers.mechanism: Friction‐induced oxidation forms a transient protective film whose eventual stress accumulation and cyclic shear causes spallation, exposing the underlying multi‐phase microstructure to enhanced wear as mechanical degradation feeds back into accelerated oxidation and spalling.

papers.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy produced by spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Performed reciprocating wear tests from ambient temperature up to 900 °C with detailed phase analysis (XRD) and wear track characterization.
papers.findings: A protective oxide film (e.g., spinel phase) was formed at elevated temperatures, which correlated with a decrease in wear depth at the highest temperatures; however, transient oxide phenomena and unstable oxide layer formation were observed at intermediate temperatures.
papers.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, oxide layer formation impacts wear behavior; a protective film may reduce wear, but if cyclic stresses during sliding cause the oxide to spall or delaminate, then exposed substrates undergo accelerated degradation.

papers.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.
papers.system: Ni-based complex concentrated alloy engineered for nanohierarchical architecture
papers.approach: Integrated nanoindentation, microstructural (glaze layer, nano-coupled grains) and friction tests across a broad temperature range (RT to 800 °C) to evaluate adaptive friction interface protection.
papers.findings: At elevated temperatures, the alloy developed a dense glaze layer that significantly reduced wear depth. However, when the protective oxide/glaze layer was imperfect (e.g., in counterparts with less optimal architecture), regions of adhesive and oxidative wear were observed.
papers.mechanism: Adaptive friction interface protection where the formation and retention of a nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes stress concentration is crucial; failure or delamination of this layer under severe conditions can result in accelerated degradation through coupled spallation and oxidative wear.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a dual-phase lamellar (FCC+BCC/B2) structure
papers.approach: Employed electrochemical tests, XPS, and electron back-scattering diffraction to evaluate passive film stability and phase-specific corrosion during immersion in chloride-containing acidic solutions at various temperatures.
papers.findings: At elevated temperature, the passive film became unstable with increased chloride attack causing pitting, particularly on the B2 phase enriched in Al and Ni, thereby provoking microgalvanic effects between phases.
papers.mechanism: The inherent microstructural heterogeneity in the eutectic HEA produces differential passive film formation and breakdown; when combined with thermal activation and mechanical wear (which can remove parts of the oxide film), local galvanic cells accelerate the coupled corrosion-wear degradation.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coatings with boron microalloying on Q235 steel substrates
papers.approach: Laser cladding to fabricate coatings with varying B content, followed by tribological and electrochemical evaluations to link microstructure changes to wear and corrosion behavior.
papers.findings: Boron addition retained the original phases while promoting TiB2 formation and lattice distortion; optimal B levels produced refined microstructure and improved oxide film stability, thereby mitigating wear and corrosion, whereas excessive TiB2 led to defects in the passive film.
papers.mechanism: Microalloying adjusts the balance between oxide film formation and microstructural integrity; an optimized oxide film can resist both mechanical spallation and corrosive attack, though imbalance leads to accentuated degradation.

established: High-entropy alloys exhibit multiphase eutectic structures that impart a complex interplay between mechanical and electrochemical behaviors.
At elevated temperatures, friction induces oxidation leading to the formation of protective oxide films, yet these films may accumulate stress and spall.
Microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., differences between FCC and BCC/B2 phases) can result in microgalvanic corrosion, enhancing localized degradation.
Alloying strategies (addition of elements like B, Mo, Ti) are effective in modifying phase stability and protective film characteristics.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying laser power during laser cladding to adjust microstructure and phase distribution
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimized energy density improved uniformity and enhanced wear resistance by forming a favorable oxide layer; inadequate energy led to heterogeneous structures prone to spallation.

approaches_tried.approach: Spark plasma sintering to produce fine multiphase microstructures in HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved dense, multiphase alloys with tunable wear properties; higher temperatures promoted protective oxide formation but also risked oxide spallation.
Enhanced both wear and corrosion resistance by refining phases and stabilizing the protective oxide; excessive microalloying induced defects.
Demonstrated that higher temperatures lead to passive film breakdown and pitting corrosion, especially due to microgalvanic effects in eutectic microstructures.

mechanisms: Friction-induced oxidation forms a protective film that may fail due to cyclic shear and stress accumulation leading to spallation.
Differential phase behavior in multiphase eutectic alloys creates microgalvanic cells, especially when one phase forms a less protective oxide.
Adaptive friction interface protection where formation of a dense glaze layer can mitigate wear, but its disruption accelerates degradation.
disagreements: While some studies emphasize the beneficial role of the oxide film in reducing friction and wear, others note that its spallation under thermal and mechanical stresses triggers accelerated degradation.
There is a debate on whether high temperatures primarily enhance protective oxide formation or instead exacerbate film instability and subsequent microgalvanic corrosion.
open_questions: Can a single mechanistic hypothesis fully reconcile the interplay between mechanically induced oxide film spallation and microgalvanic corrosion in multi-phase eutectic HEAs?
How does the coupling of wear and corrosion processes evolve over longer service times under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads?
What is the quantitative contribution of each phase's individual response (e.g., FCC vs. B2) to the combined degradation rate under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions?
opportunities: Design controlled experiments comparing eutectic HEAs with matched single-phase versions under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures to distinguish the effect of microstructural heterogeneity.
Implement in situ monitoring techniques (e.g., high-temperature microscopy or spectroscopy) to capture the kinetics of oxide film formation, spallation, and subsequent corrosion.
Explore alloying combinations that optimize phase distribution and oxide film stability (such as controlled additions of B, Mo, or Ti) to balance mechanical resistance and corrosion protection.
Investigate time-dependent evolution of microgalvanic coupling at phase interfaces to develop models that predict total degradation as a function of wear and corrosion rates.

directions.direction: Friction‐induced transient oxide film spallation that exposes heterogeneous phases
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the coupling between wear‐induced mechanical removal and thermal oxidation. The evidence shows that frictional heating leads to an oxide film formation that later spalls under cyclic shear (e.g., PMC12156342::web::036::3_2_mechanical_properties). The physics of stress accumulation within an oxide film are well understood, and the approach is experimentally feasible using in situ wear testing and oxide characterization.

directions.direction: Differential passive film stability on constituent phases leading to microgalvanic corrosion
directions.assessment: This direction focuses on how the multiphase (e.g., FCC vs. BCC/B2) microstructure yields different oxide properties so that galvanic cells form at phase boundaries. It is supported by evidence on microgalvanic effects (PMC9319277::web::022::3_4_corrosion_observation) and meets the constraints by addressing simultaneous wear and corrosion at high temperatures. Controlled electrochemical and microscopic comparisons are feasible.

directions.direction: Cyclic mechanical loading causing repeated oxide formation and brittle delamination
directions.assessment: This direction hypothesizes that cyclic stress at elevated temperature repeatedly forms and then mechanically damages the oxide layers; the cycle disrupts passivation and accelerates both adhesive wear and corrosion. The evidence from tribological studies (PMC10241162::web::015::remarkable_wear_resistance_and_wear_mech) supports such dynamic processes. It is a direct and measurable mechanism with a controlled comparison between cyclic and static loading.

directions.direction: Interphase boundary stress concentration driving localized cracking and preferential degradation
directions.assessment: This approach posits that the intrinsic microstructural heterogeneity in a eutectic HEA results in stress concentration at phase interfaces; under elevated temperature and wear, these areas crack, leading to rapid oxide fracture and localized corrosion. It leverages differences between single-phase and multiphase HEAs and is supported by evidence showing phase-specific corrosion (PMC12735082::web::019::4_conclusions). The approach is experimentally feasible and falsifiable via comparative degradation tests.
